I think one of the stumbling blocks for those who have come to repentance via their genuine sorrow for sins, those that hit bottom, so to speak, seeing their lives and relationships destroyed by their own selfish and destructive behavior, and having a rocky path to making things right, is that there are resentments for those who come to the faith by other means.

There are many who are raised Christian, in godly homes, and can't even tell you when they believed.

There are many who, when they heard the truth, accepted it. Absent trauma or drama, and yet saved.

There are those who had long ago cleaned up their act, dealt with their addictions, or put away the anger and hurt at being victimized, say by abuse, physical, sexual or emotional. That turned over a new leaf, and yet only believed on the Gospel years after.

And there are those, caught in the jaws of addiction, struggling to get out, long after repenting of what led them there, but unable to break free, who are comforted by a believer, and asking them, are given the Gospel and while yet, still sinners, in a moment of clarity, believe.

People who crawled through whatever hell on earth to come to salvation, by sorrow for their sin, can look at these disparate cases, and others like them, and think "that person is not really saved, like I am."

And the promotion of the idea that we must repent of our sins to be saved feeds that resentment, and can make a repentant heart grow bitter over time.

teachings.title: Repentance of sin breeds hypocrisy and testimonial pride
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: Emphasising what one turned from instead of what one turned to creates a caste of the more saved, fruit inspectors and boastful testimonials, when all were equally damned and saved by grace alone.
teachings.text:
This resentment is similar to the workers who labored all day for the same penny that those late arrivals collected in the parable Jesus tells in Matthew 20. It's sort of the inverse reaction of the good son in the parable of the prodigal son.

It's this attitude that leads to holier than thou fruit inspectors, judging others salvation by their works, being a respecter of persons regarding testimonials, etc.

Before heading in to Matthew chapter 23, it's a good idea to consider how hypocrisy flourishes from the idea of salvation by repentance from sin, rather than repentance towards God and faith in Christ.

By placing the emphasis on what was turned from, rather than the testimony of what is turned to, what the changing of mind has wrought through faith, it creates an almost inevitable form of a caste system within a church. Of respecters of persons, who in hypocrisy see themselves as *more saved* than others.

Just as the apostles asking Jesus of whose sin was responsible for the man blind from birth, or those questioning him about the men killed by Pilate, are those who had a wall fall on them killing them, the tendency and inclination to place the path to righteousness some take over the experience of others is the same form of hypocrisy which Jesus warns us against.

For all have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God. For all were perishing before repenting to believe on Christ. For all are deserving of hell, and none are justified by their works of the law.

We are all in the same boat and there but for the grace of God go each and every one of us. Regardless of how relatively easy we came to salvation, and regardless of how we struggle to pick up our cross daily and follow him.

And losing sight of that leads to our focusing on the mote of our neighbor's eye. Of neglecting the beam in our own. Of judging in hypocrisy the Christian walk of others, while neglecting to work out our own salvation in fear and trembling.

This is one reason why I dislike so-called testimonial preaching. Not the testimony of Jesus Christ and the saving power of faith, but the long winded testimonials, almost reveling in past sin, showing you just how down low someone was before receiving the gospel, almost a point of pride of how much they had to dig themselves out to get to where others are mercifully, by the grace of God.

And I have been in churches where this becomes almost a competition of sorts. And where people blessed to have been born into a Godly family, and whose sowing of wild oats was almost incidental, making it out to be that they were low down wretched creatures, by way of showing just how really super duper saved they are, through their "struggle." Who haven't been blessed by God's grace and mercy, are embarrassed by it, for the glory that is heaped upon those with a testimony of a life of sin, turned around.

This is yet another reason why Satan has painstakingly and methodically brainwashed everyone into adding "...of sin" to repentance. It's another way this becomes toxic in even good churches, with the right Gospel.

We should not glory in the fact that those more sinful than we were saved. We should glory in God that he would save any of us. We were all equally damned. We all had to turn to believe the same thing to gain life. One sin or millions. A degenerate life in the swinehurd, for a life of ease and comfort of our father's estate.

For all have fallen short of the glory of God and deserve death and Hell.

But God has sent his servants to invite us to his Son's wedding feast, both good and bad, called to repentance. Amen

teachings.title: Verses misused for repenting of sin
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: Ezekiel 14, Luke 13 and Revelation 9, rightly divided, are about national judgment, misunderstanding, and unbelief, not repenting of sins to be born again.
teachings.text:
It's easy to understand, by looking at verses commonly cited as supporting the false damnable heresy of repentance of sin for salvation, to see precisely what is being repented of in each.

Ezekiel 14:6

*Therefore say unto the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Repent, and turn yourselves from your idols; and turn away your faces from all your abominations.*

First, let us rightly divide the word of God here, it isn't regarding salvation of a person's soul, rather this is directed at the nation of Israel which had put their faith in idols, facing the abominations set before them in service to false gods.

God speaking through the prophet is telling them that they will be judged as a nation if they do not repent of false belief in idols.

Or **Luke 13**

*There were present at that season some that told him of the Galilaeans, whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices.*

*2 And Jesus answering said unto them, Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things?*

*3 I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.*

*4 Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?*

*5 I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.*

*6 He spake also this parable; A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard; and he came and sought fruit thereon, and found none.*

*7 Then said he unto the dresser of his vineyard, Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?*

*8 And he answering said unto him, Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it:*

*9 And if it bear fruit, well: and if not, then after that thou shalt cut it down.*

Jesus isn't telling them to repent of their sins, he's reminding them that they are as sinful as those they are judging. That people who have suffered a bitter end, in this case being killed by Pilate or in a construction accident were no more or less sinners than they were. And they need to repent of that misunderstanding of how things work, because it is a stumbling block to their acceptance of salvation.

**Revelation 9**

*20 And the rest of the men which were not killed by these plagues yet repented not of the works of their hands, that they should not worship devils, and idols of gold, and silver, and brass, and stone, and of wood: which neither can see, nor hear, nor walk:*

*21 Neither repented they of their murders, nor of their sorceries, nor of their fornication, nor of their thefts.*

Again, this verse isn't about individual soul salvation. What we are witnessing is God's wrath pouring out on the unbelievers that remained on the Earth, and that despite all the horrors being poured out upon them, including the plague of hellish locust creatures, the unbelieving didn't repent of their unbelief, they didn't turn from their idols or their wickedness to be saved, physically from the wrath.

Using these three instances as an example of repenting of your sins to be born again, shows a lack of spiritual discernment and understanding of scripture. Don't be fooled.

teachings.title: I changed my mind about how to be saved
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: No one needs to change his mind that sin is wrong, since conscience already tells him; real repentance is changing one's mind about what must be done to be saved and believing on Christ's blood.
teachings.text:
How can you change your mind about sin when we all know, from the law written in our hearts, from our conscience, from the rebuke and reproach of the Holy Ghost that all unsaved men feel, having the knowledge of right and wrong. Being past any age of accountability.

I didn't repent of sin to be saved because I've never thought sin was good or right. I've never changed my mind about that, I've always known it's wrong.

But thank God and praise Jesus, I changed my mind about what I needed to do to be saved, and believed on the blood of the Lamb that washes away sins, and the gift of eternal life.

That's real repentance in order to be born again.

teachings.title: Repented not, that ye might believe him
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: The parable of the two sons shows Biblical repentance is turning to believe God's word, which the publicans and harlots did and the self-righteous chief priests did not.
teachings.text:
Next Jesus is again tempted by the Pharisees, asking "*By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority?"* And again, Jesus confounds them by asking them to answer by what authority do they say came John the Baptist.

*If we shall say, From heaven; he will say unto us, Why did ye not then believe him? But if we shall say, Of men; we fear the people; for all hold John as a prophet. And they answered Jesus, and said, We cannot tell. And he said unto them, Neither tell I you by what authority I do these things.*

Then Jesus questions them by way of a parable. A certain man with two sons, orders them to work his vineyard. One refuses, but changes his mind and goes to work. The other days yes, but doesn't do it. Which did the the will of the father?

They rightly say the first, not seeing the meaning and Jesus readily gives it to them, but good.

*Verily I say unto you, That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you. For John came unto you in the way of righteousness, and ye believed him not: but the publicans and the harlots believed him: and ye, when ye had seen it, repented not afterward, that ye might believe him.*

We see again, Biblical repentance is a turning towards belief in what God tells us is His will. Faith in His word. Jesus tells these self-righteousness holy men that the worst sinners who believed John that the kingdom of God was at hand are the first son, and they the second, claiming they do the will of the Father but did it not, not believing him who He sent.

And to drive the point home even further, Jesus tells them another parable, of the certain householder, who doing all the work, created a great vineyard, and hired husbandmen to tend it and left it to them to bring in the harvest to him.

And when time came, the man sent his servants to collect the increase from the husbandmen, and they beat them, killed them. Stoned them. And more servants were sent, and they did likewise.

Finally, the man sent his son, that they would receive him with due reverence. But, seeking to steal his inheritance and keep it for themselves, cast out the son and slew him.

Jesus asks them what should this lord do to the traitorous husbandmen, and they destroy them and hire those who will render what's due, the fruits of the field.

And so, condemned by their own words, unable to come to repentance, having beaten and slain the prophets, and soon to have taken the Son to do the same, Jesus upbraided these vipers.

*Jesus saith unto them, Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?*

*Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof. And whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder.*

And finally understanding He was speaking of them, they wanted to seize Jesus and kill Him, but were afraid of the crowd that had been singing hosannas to Him, calling Him a prophet. The very thing they sought to accuse Jesus with in the beginning, now what held them back at this time.

teachings.title: Repenting from dead works, not of sin
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: The unrepentant are those who trust their own turning from sin instead of repenting from dead works toward the free gift of faith in Christ's finished work.
teachings.text:
The unrepentant are those that hear the Gospel of faith, and refuse to obey it. Who won't turn from their dead works and their vain traditions, towards the gift of grace from God through Christ.

Who place their ability or willingness to turn from sin as their means of justification, or retaining the imputed righteousness of Jesus, despite being told by the word of God, over and over again that they must. That it is repenting from dead works and towards that free gift of salvation by faith in the perfect work of Christ that justifies us. That it is being born again, quickened in spirit, that leads us from sin.

Confusing discipleship and sanctification of the believer with justification and obtaining righteousness, they receive none of it.

Their works as filthy rags, wood hay and stubble that is burned away, leaving them perishing. Because they couldn't obey the Gospel of reconciliation, and so they remain perishing.

*Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.*

And so, trapped in what the Bible calls the bondage of the law, pursuing salvation through "repentance of sin," a concept not found in the Gospel, but warned against throughout the New Testament, they like the Judaizers of the 1st century place their faith in themselves. And truly unrepentant, will die in their sin.

teachings.title: Repent and turn to God
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: Paul's repent and turn to God, and do works meet for repentance, means turning one's trust from false beliefs and works to God, then doing works fitting for that turning.
teachings.text:
Paul says he showed the truth of the Gospel *first unto them of Damascus, and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the coasts of Judaea, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, and do works meet for repentance. For these causes the Jews caught me in the temple, and went about to kill me.*

We see Biblical repentance in regards to salvation is turning from what ever is being believed in regards to God's word, and turning towards God for salvation. That, as we have seen again and again, it's always used in this fashion. That the "...of sin," or whatever isn't mentioned. It is turning your trust from false beliefs, your own works, false gods and idols, and towards God. And once saved doing works suitable and proper for such a turning.

This, Paul says is why the Jews want him dead, as the book of Acts has shown us again and again. This message of hope and good news of the resurrection, and their role in killing Christ, and their resentment at losing the inheritance to the Gentiles has always been why the Jew persecutest God's people.

Even today, making Gentiles unworthy of God's inheritance is their goal, and the subversive nature of the Jew is dedicated to this cause, and preventing those of us who have obtained our portion of the kingdom of God from giving others the same adoption of faith.

teachings.title: Repent of trusting anything but Christ
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: Romans, John and Acts consistently show salvation by faith alone for all who believe, so what must be repented of is trusting anything besides the finished work of Christ.
teachings.text:
Just understand, that in the study I've been doing here, the entire book of Romans, The Gospel of John, and now halfway through the book of Acts and we have seen consistently that salvation is by faith alone, that it is offered to all who believe, and it is not contingent on denomination or our ability to repent from sin.

This is why you must read the Bible and get your Doctrine from God, not from men. Comparing scripture with scripture, studying to find yourself approved by God.

If you have placed your trust in anything else besides the perfect work of Christ Jesus, who lived, suffered and died, went to hell for three days and three nights carrying the burden of all sin, and was risen again to take his place at the right hand of the Father, this is what you must repent of. This is what you need to change your mind about and accept what the scriptures tell you is the simplicity of The Good news, The Gospel of Jesus Christ. The word of God.

teachings.title: Repentance unto life is turning to the Lord
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: Acts 11 uses granted repentance unto life and turned unto the Lord for the same thing, so biblical repentance is turning to the Lord, with no implied from sin.
teachings.text:
Acts 11 opens with Peter's return from Caesarea, and the centurion Cornelius' home, where many Gentiles were saved and given gifts of the Holy Ghost, similar to the disciples on Pentecost. This news excites some, but many who were saved of the Jews, those of the circumcision, were appalled he made company with the uncircumcised, giving them the Gospel and eating with them.

These were special boys, respecter of persons and Peter retells the events that led to it, and God revealing they must preach to the Gentiles as much as the Jews scattered abroad. "*What was I, that I could withstand God?*"

Peter's vision and the events that followed, and the witness of the 6 who sojourned with him to Caesarea is sufficient an explanation for them to stifle their complaints and glorify God.

"*Then hath God also to the Gentiles granted repentance unto life.*"

This realization brings the scattered disciples, who had been preaching in synagogues to diaspora Jews throughout the world to turn their nets to the other side of the boat, and being fishers of men, winning many Gentiles to Christ.

"*And the hand of the Lord was with them: and a great number believed, and turned unto the Lord.*"

Note that verse 18 and 22, both quoted above, state similar things. 18 using "repentance," 21 "turned unto."

They have identical meaning. There is no implied "...from sin." It is Biblical repentance, *turning to the Lord.*

We see the establishment of local churches, and that in Antioch they were first called Christians.

We are told of Barnabas journey to Tarsus to seek out Saul, and the beginning of their epic if sometime contentious partnership in church planting and evangelizing for Christ.

teachings.title: We all sin every day
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: Since we all sin daily, repenting from sin for righteousness is foolish; God forgives us in Jesus' name, and the Spirit and word help us overcome sin for our edification.
teachings.text:
Drinking is a sin. So is eating that extra cupcake. So are thoughts of foolishness. We all sin every day. The idea we can "Repent from sin" for righteousness is itself a foolish thought.

We wrestle with the flesh daily, we are called to crucify ourselves daily. To mortify our members and being ourselves into subjection. To strive for that prize of rewards in Heaven by doing God's work which is honoring Him, spreading the good news of Jesus Christ and taking care of and being a good judge of the poor, lame, widows and fatherless.

God knows we are in sinful flesh and He forgives us in Jesus name, and the Spirit and His word are there to help us overcome sin as Christ overcame the world, to our own edification and to be conformed to His use.

teachings.title: Simon the sorcerer repents as a believer
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: Peter's rebuke to Simon to repent of his wickedness was to an already saved man who sinned, not a condition of salvation, and the laying on of hands gave gifts, not the indwelling Spirit.
teachings.text:
So forgive me for almost skipping chapter 8, because it is a good one.

We see Saul again, fresh from being the coat holder for the Jews who stoned Stephen to death, and are told he consented of that evil. The Bible says being a partaker in another man's sin is as bad as commiting it ourselves. Saul, in his ignorance embraces the persecution of the believers in Jerusalem and in all of Judea, zealously thinking he is doing it for God, that the saints were blasphemous doing what they did in Jesus' name.

We see once again that in persecution, all things work together for good to them that love God, and God in their affliction uses the scattering to bring the truth of the Gospel out of Jerusalem and into the whole world.

Phillip, one of the deacons selected with Stephen and whom the Apostles laid hands on, filling him with the gifts of the Holy Ghost goes to Samaria, the capital of the province that was once the Northern Kingdom of Israel, before God used the Syrians to wipe them out. There, there are a mix of followers of the Hebrew religious practices, who followed scripture and knew of Christ to come, and unbelievers from every background. It was this mixed race mess that caused the Jews to look down on Samaritans, despite their cultural and racial similarities and origin.

Phillip has tremendous success in getting Samaritans saved, through his preaching and the miracles of healing and casting out devils through the power of the Holy Ghost imparted to him by the Apostles and the laying on of hands.

We meet Simon, AKA Simon the sorcerer, a charlatan who had great fame in the land, but who did trick people into believing he had some power from God. But his paltry parlor tricks were nothing compared to the truth of the word and the power of God moving through Philip, and as the masses believed on Christ, Simon too became saved, born again in faith and even joining Philip in his ministries.

When the Apostles hear of the great things of God Philip was doing among the Samaritans, they went up to see and give the gift of the Holy Ghost upon the believers that they may continue to grow the church there and bring people to salvation.

It is important to understand the difference between the quickening and indwelling of the Spirit upon belief and salvation, and the doctrine of laying on of hands. All believers were born again and had the Spirit inside them with the new man created at the time of their salvation, but the gifts of the Holy Ghost, in the Old Testament sense of having Him come over one and grant them power, was something that the Apostles were granted by Jesus, and given unto them to share as needed to the glory of God.

Simon seeing their ability to imbue others with this great power, and perhaps missing the glory he had in the past, coveted it, and sought to pay Peter and John for the same gift earning a harsh rebuke from Peter, telling Simon to get his heart right with God. He tells Simon to repent of this wickedness and pray for forgiveness.

Many grace-mixing works heretics point to this, one of the few times "repent" is followed by anything close to "of sins" as proof text for their false doctrine, but in doing so they omit that Simon was already saved. He believed on Jesus already. He did something wicked, but his repentance isn't for righteousness but as a believer who has sinned.

And showing the conviction of his salvation, Simon accepts the rebuke and repents. Often you will see unbelievers, even those who claim Christ, bristle at correction. As the Bible says they despise it. But Simon, to his credit learns and grows from it.

teachings.title: Repent and be baptized: the order of things
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: In Acts 2:38 Peter calls the Jews to repent of their unbelief in the Christ they crucified, then be baptized, so it teaches neither repenting of sins nor baptism for remission.
teachings.text:
Continuing the Gospel, Peter tells them of the resurrection, Jesus overcoming death, and points to Psalm 16 where David writing in the Spirit, gives prophecy of Jesus. Peter reminds them that David wasn't speaking of himself as his body was buried in the sepiculture. That David was speaking of Christ to come, which the disciples were testifying they had seen risen, first hand.

Peter explains that having fulfilled God's promise, they had received the Holy Ghost, and the masses witness of this miracle of the tongues is evidence that all of this is true.

*Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made the same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ.*

Hearing the Gospel and the truth of the good news and changing their minds, accepting the truth, understanding the role they played in killing the Son of God, they believed. And they asked "what shall we do?"

Peter replies "*repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.*"

Note the order of things. Peter gives them the Gospel. They ask what they now must do. Peter tells them repent, or change their mind. Not "of sin" but of what they, *in ignorance* and *unbelief* did, participating in His death. That they believe. Then they should be baptized in Jesus' name. Proving their belief. That they will have remission of sins and the gift of the Holy Ghost from that change of mind, of their repentance to believing on Him.

This statement confuses the unsaved as much as anything else in the Bible. They isolate it, out of context to teach repent of sins heresy and the false understanding that baptism is what gives us remission of sins, despite multiple examples throughout scripture that it is the belief and calling upon the name of the Lord that gives us salvation. That remission of sins comes from Christ Jesus, not of the works or rites we do.

Stripped of all context, including who Peter is speaking to, what they did, the unbelief they shared and why they must repent from it, to accept Jesus as the Christ, many are led astray.

Peter and the other 120 continue soul winning the crowd, exhorting them to *save themselves from this untoward generation*.

They that received the good news and believed were then baptized. (Again note the order of operations).

And so 120 saved 3,000. What's wonderful about this is those souls were from all nations on earth, and so God having created this feast of the first fruits, created the way for the news of the Gospel to be spread to every corner of the world, 1,300yrs before this fateful day.

teachings.title: John 3:16 has no and
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: John 3 says nothing of repenting of sins, Lordship, works, church or baptism to be saved, and so refutes those heresies and TULIP.
teachings.text:
Oh I feel like Colombo here, but one more thing.

Notice there is absolutely zero mention, not in word or in meaning, of repentance of sin to be saved.

John 3:16 does not say "for God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten son that whoever believeth on him and repent of their sins, shall not perish..." And it doesn't say "who makes Jesus "Lord of their life."

I meant to mention that in the commentary. John 3 destroys heresies like TULIP, that everlasting isn't everlasting, that you have to repent of sins, do works, belong to the right church, be baptized, baptism of infants, by sprinkling, dispensationalism, modalism, that Jesus never preached about being God, the Son of God, or His crucifixion.

There are probably other false doctrines and errors it destroys but you get the gist.

teachings.title: What the Bible means by repent
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: Going through the repentance verses in context shows none requires turning from sin to be saved; repentance for salvation is changing the mind to believe the gospel.
teachings.text:
**2 Chronicles 7:14** - *If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.* (Nation turning from sin. Not about salvation)

**Proverbs 28:13** - *He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy*.
(Confessing/giving up sin. Not about salvation)

**Ezekiel 18:21-23** - *But if the wicked will turn from all his sins that he hath committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die.*   (Turn from sin. Keep all statutes and laws for salvation challenge, impossible)*

**Matthew 4:17** - *From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand*. (Change mind)

**Luke 13:3** - *I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.*(context of reproaching holier than thou/trusting in works)

**Acts 2:38** - *Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.* (Context, Pentecost sermon to Jews, repent from not believing Jesus was the Christ whom they just killed and had been raised)

**Acts 3:19** - Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord; (context Repent of being ignorant of who Christ was that they and their leaders had killed)

**Acts 17:30** - *And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent*: (context: repent of the ignorance God had winked at, enumerated in previous verses, worshipping false gods)

**Romans 2:4 -** *Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?* (Context: saved not being inexcusable hypocrites, grace of God go I. Repentance synonymous with believing gospel, not linked to sin)

**2 Peter 3:9** - *The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance*. (Not linked to turning from sin, but believing)

**Revelation 2:5** - *Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.* (Already saved church members, turn from being slack in doing the first works. Not salvation)

The only verse here that could possibly be taken as requiring turning away from sin to be saved is Ezekiel, and we know for individual salvation sinless perfection is impossible, because of the rest of the Bible tells us that the only way to be saved by the law is to not offend, even one point, but there's none righteous, no not one.

To receive the free gift of salvation must agree that we are sinners, that we cannot be righteous on our own, that we deserve death and Hell, but that God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son that whoever shall believe on Him shall not perish but have everlasting life that can never be lost. If you don't believe this, repent, for the kingdom of God is at hand.

teachings.title: No verse says quit sin to be saved
teachings.theme: Repentance is a change of mind
teachings.summary: There is no clear verse making giving up sin a condition of salvation, so it is not doctrine, since doctrine must come from clear scripture, not men.
teachings.text:
This quick bible study on the concept of repentance in the Bible isn't exhaustive however, it is conclusive. There is no clear verse that spells out a Doctrine that says that we must give up sin or be willing to give up sin in order to believe and be saved. Repentance is a changing of mind or turning from one thing to another.

I left out the verses where it says God repented. No one would say God repented of his sin because God is sinless.

And as I'm trying to express in this channel when dealing with mistaken ideas, error, and damnable heresies, unless you have a clear verse that says precisely what it is you're saying as Doctrine, that doesn't contradict anything else in the Bible, then it's wrong.

We get our Doctrine from scripture, not men.

teachings.title: There is none righteous, no, not one
teachings.summary: Psalm 14, quoted in Romans 3, is the definitive statement that all have sinned and need the gospel, and that the fool denies the God he knows.
teachings.text:
The opening 3 verses of **Psalm 14** stand as the definitive and true statements of the doctrine that all men have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God. Quoted in part by Paul in **Romans 3:10–12**
*As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one: There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God. They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one*.

It serves as a universal appeal to the need for the gospel, and the reconciliation of fallen men with a holy God. There is none good but God. All have gone astray.

The opening verse is an even deeper truth, showing the self-deception that leads fools to claim there is no God. They may say this, but ultimately every man knows that God is, and the judge of all things.

Like the scribes and Pharisees that Jesus preaches against in **Matthew 23**, these fools, the workers of iniquity, devour the poor. They eat up the people as bread.

They call not upon the Lord. They shame the counsel of the poor, they profane the hope of the righteous, they deny the Lord that bought them.

teachings.title: Not a just man upon earth that sinneth not
teachings.summary: There is not a just man that sinneth not, the foundation of the gospel, so the fear of God humbles us to see our own sin and seek His grace.
teachings.text:
Continuing in **Ecclesiastes 7**, where Solomon the Preacher has built upon the truth that the toil and tribulation of life is vain and vexing, his observation that despite this, God has blessed men to enjoy the fruits of that labor. He has shown that it is better to be reminded of the short span man's life is, that death comes for us all, wise or fool, rich or poor.

That, despite the seeming vanity of life, the pointlessness of endless striving, that the blessing of God makes it bearable and that this blessing comes on the righteous and the wise, while the foolish and froward, greedy and lazy see their efforts come to nothing in the end.

And so, picking up in v15, the Preacher concedes that he has seen the wicked prosper and the righteous perish. That there are other factors that determine the outcome. That the just man may see a short life, while the unrighteous may prolong their time under the Sun.

But generally speaking, the just and wise are blessed more than the fool and the wicked.

From this he argues temperance, and against self-righteous displays of piety, or becoming self-important in your wisdom. Why tempt God? And don't be wicked or foolish, because again, God will repay.

It isn't the appearance that brings life, but the genuine fear of God. The key understanding is sincere and humble respect for the Lord. The rest takes care of itself.

The strength of wisdom is true, and can be relied on, but the truth of the matter is we all fall short. For all have sinned.

v20 *For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not.*

This wisdom is the foundation of the gospel. We are all sinners before a holy God. So even in appearance of righteousness, we have sin. Even in the strength of wisdom, we've all done foolishly. Thus, what the Lord decides is just, is just.

It is hypocrisy to think more of ourselves than we should. An honest inventory, examining ourselves as we are instructed to do, reveals that we too have fallen short.

We have cursed others. We have held hatred in our hearts. We have dealt unfairly, the iniquity we see in the wicked has had a home in our hearts.

Fear of God humbles us to know our own heart. Acknowledging this truth of ourselves, the course of the wicked and the just, revealed by the wrath of God from heaven, and His mercy and longsuffering towards us, we should humbly seek His grace.

teachings.title: I shall go to him
teachings.summary: David's comfort at his infant's death shows young children who die are with Christ, refuting the teaching that original sin condemns infants.
teachings.text:
And so David's son is stricken with illness, and for seven days the king refuses to eat or any comfort, hoping that God may repent and spare his son. But on the 7th day, his infant child dies. The servants are hesitant to tell the king, but David sees their whispering and asks is the child dead, and they say yes.

David arises from his mourning and asks for food, and the servants are amazed that he took the news so well. But David says, while the boy lived he hoped that the Lord might turn from his judgement, but now that he's dead he knows he will someday see him again.

This is the comfort we have in the death of a young child. That they are with Christ in Heaven.

It is curious that many professing Christians teach the lie of original sin condemning infants, innocents who have not sinned themselves, and will often use **Psalm 51** to do it, while the Psalm was written by David during his despair, saying he himself was wicked beyond measure, using hyperbole to describe his own condition in this very matter, not to condemn his own child.

teachings.title: Little ones with no knowledge of good and evil
teachings.summary: Deuteronomy 1 shows an age of accountability, children being innocent without the law, against the original sin teaching behind infant baptism.
teachings.text:
Beginning **Deuteronomy**, which means 'second law,' Moses retelling of the events that led the Israelites to the verge of the promised land, and the restatement of the law of God. The events retold in this chapter are familiar to us, having just finished **Numbers**. But there is still doctrine to be found.

**Deuteronomy 1** has the clearest proof text on the idea that there is an age of accountability. That children do not carry some original sin, as some insist falsely, but are innocent without the law.

*Moreover your little ones, which ye said should be a prey, and your children, which in that day had no knowledge between good and evil, they shall go in thither, and unto them will I give it, and they shall possess it.*

This isn't a set age, but a spiritual condition. For some, the realization between good and evil comes younger, some older. Some developmentally disabled, it may never come at all.

This idea is reflected in Paul's writing, in **Romans 7:9**

**For I was alive without the law once: but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died.**

The concept of infants being born with sin is a wicked one, but required by the apostate false churches that teach baby "baptism" in order to make a lifetime claim on a soul, to exert power and control over the masses. The heresy of baptismal regeneration leads to it, and for mothers especially, the idea that their baby could pass and end up in hell or "limbo" was too much to bear. And silly women carried away by false doctrine, like Eve, lead their men to stray. And so, heretical practices take root, and damnable ones at that.

**Matthew 18:2-4**
*And Jesus called a little child unto him, and set him in the midst of them, and said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, the same is greatest in the kingdom of heaven.*

We need to humble ourselves as children to receive the grace of salvation. Knowing we are helpless in obtaining our own righteousness and totally reliant on the Father.

teachings.title: By one man sin entered
teachings.summary: Adam's one sin brought death, not an inherited original sin, the law came to show sin abounding, and by one man Christ grace abounds to all who believe.
teachings.text:
The first law was to Adam, and it was simple. Do not eat of the fruit of the tree in the midst of the garden. For you will surely die.

And Adam broke the single law in paradise. And by his sin, death came up on the world. Paradise was denied us, and the way of the world, short and brutish lives. And sin multiplied, and death. All through one man.

This is not original sin, btw. There is no sin that follows man from birth, but only the understanding that it is in our nature, even under perfect conditions as Eden, that we still fall short.

And so the law came, to Noah, to Abraham, to Moses, and by Sinai, so detailed and expanded, much more than the single commandment of the Garden, so that man had to know that the holiness of God was unattainable by their works, and that faith in His grace alone was our only hope.

And with the law, sin abounded much the more, that God's grace may abound to His glory.

So that by one man, the man Christ Jesus, and His righteousness and His willingness to die for us, and not only those who believe, but for every man and all sin, he gave His life that we may enter into peace with the Father by faith, in His grace. To His glory. That the righteousness of God be shown the world.

teachings.title: Let God be true, but every man a liar
teachings.summary: The Jews' advantage of the oracles did not save them, unbelief does not void God's faithfulness, grace is no license to sin, and all are under sin.
teachings.text:
Continuing the methodical building of Paul's arguments, from chapter 1 and 2; that Gentiles without the law are without excuse, and Jews with the law are without excuse, that the revelation of God is given us naturally as well as scripture and the prophets, that the truth of God is found in His wrath against those He rejects, and His judgment on sin is the same on all men, regardless of being a Jew or a Gentile, circumcision or uncircumcission. That we are worthy of death and we fear His judgment knowing it is correct (even as others knowing that what they do is deserving death, do it anyway and take pleasure in others sin), that the law could save if man didn't sin...Chapter 3 opens with the final stipulations leading to what is the clearest presentation of the doctrine of salvation in scripture.

He concedes that while God is not a respecter of persons, the Jews did indeed have an advantage, having the law spelled out for them. The profit of circumcision, not the act itself but of being a Hebrew under the law, had the oracles of God committed unto them. They had Moses and the prophets. The temple and the scriptures. And the Jews who didn't believe the word, and rejected and killed Christ do not nullify the faith of God, which is true even in man's unbelief. Let God be true, but every man a liar. The righteousness of God isn't dependent on our righteousness and isn't undone by our unrighteousness. And by keeping the truth of God rather than the lies of man, we shall overcome.

Those lies include our own reasoning against the truth of God. Our own dispute of His holy judgment. Remember the sin of the reprobate is to hold that truth of God in unrighteousness. To change the truth of God into a lie. To challenge His judgment against man's sin. To condemn others while excusing ourselves and the hypocrisy of those who say they keep the law, but offend in not just one, but all points. Trusting circumcision to save them. Their ethnic identity. These are the lies of men, but let God be true, and we shall overcome in the judgment.

Paul then offers what a man may say, that if our sin, if our lies reveal His righteousness, is God wrong in His judgment? Does our sin making His holiness being shown mean His judgment against us is unrighteous?

Like, "aren't we doing Him a favor by sinning? Showing His grace, so He shouldn't judge us so harshly!" Real Natural Man hours.

God forbid. If God was unrighteous for judging the world that shows His glory in His wrath against sin, then how could He judge sin in the first place? It's a foolish argument.

Paul had been accused by some, likely works-of-the-law salvationists given the context, who slanderously reported that Paul's teaching of the Gospel of grace meant he was saying if we believe and are saved, we have a license to sin. This is a common argument made by those trusting in their works of righteousness against those teaching the Gospel of reconciliation and grace. That it is "easy believism." That we tell people since they are saved from Hell and death by "saying a prayer," we give them the ok to do whatever they want in the liberty of Christ.

 *Let us do evil, that good may come.* That the grace of God is glorified by forgiveness of the most wicked, and so be even more wicked. (There are Jewish sects that practice this, without Christ; Sabbateans and Frankists, but that's a topic for another day).

Summarizing the original point, having gone down a bit of a rabbit trail of natural man arguments against him, Paul asks the believing Jews in Rome, are they any better than the Gentiles, even with their advantage of having the law? No. In no wise. Because as he's already proven, all are under sin. All deserve death and Hell. All need salvation. None have any excuse. None have any natural advantage against the judgment of God, which is righteous and just. Even if our sin and His wrath brings to others the revelation of God's glory, even if our faith and forgiveness brings revelation of God's righteousness.

Because there is none righteous; no, not one.

teachings.title: The wickedness of man, not bloodlines
teachings.summary: The flood shows evil comes from man's own heart, not from foreign bloodlines or hybrids, so all men of one blood have free will and need salvation by faith.
teachings.text:
The story of the flood as a judgment upon mankind is clear throughout that it is man's own wickedness that God is punishing. That within 8 generations, mankind had fallen so utterly that it had corrupted the earth itself. That only Noah had stayed faithful, God's Spirit striving with him, but not so that of man.

It is humanity that has fallen. It is man that is corrupt and wicked of heart. The same as it was in the beginning as it is today.

This is an important biblical doctrine to understand.

Many false doctrines place evil as something that is 'other,' foreign, introduced by bloodlines or genetics or ancestry. That salvation is only for a certain people, elect by nothing other than genes.

But we see in Genesis 6 that it is man's own wickedness that destroys us. That our flesh is what brings us to sin. That by faith in God, man can find grace and salvation.

This is extremely important and is a tangential doctrine to the concept of free will and individual soul liberty/damnation.

If man is irredeemable by genetics, then it is by a false calvinist god. If man, is saved by an inalienable quality bestowed by a creator, then he hasn't free will. If man is judged by other's sin, he hasn't the individual soul liberty to be saved by faith in Christ, being condemned by another's actions.

Since the time of Adam in the garden, blaming his sin on Eve and God for creating her, man seeks to find an excuse to justify themselves before the Lord in His judgment.

To push it off on the devil for offering temptation. To place it on the sins of another.

But God knows our heart, and says *the thoughts of* man's *heart was only evil continually.*

There is none righteous, no not one.

And this understanding is the basis for the faith in God for salvation. The knowledge that to walk with God, to strive with His Spirit requires His grace and His promise of salvation. Not of ourselves, but as a gift of God. That we are wicked and sinful creatures, deserving death and Hell, and in need of saving.

By placing the blame on external forces, even upon the demonic lineage of quasi-human chimeras, for example, we say "maybe it's not our fault God. After all, maybe it's not our fault."

But God *hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth.* He made nations and habitations and divisions of people, but we are all one blood, given to the same temptation of the flesh, sinful nature, with free will and the need for salvation.

teachings.title: This is the gospel one must believe
teachings.theme: The gospel that must be believed
teachings.summary: The gospel to believe is Christ's death, burial and resurrection for our sins, as preached to the jailer and the eunuch, not a willingness to turn from sin.
teachings.text:
**1 Corinthians 15:1-11**
*Moreover, brethren, I declare unto you the gospel which I preached unto you, which also ye have received, and wherein ye stand; By which also ye are saved, if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain. For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures: And that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve: After that, he was seen of above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present, but some are fallen asleep. After that, he was seen of James; then of all the apostles. And last of all he was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time. For I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. Therefore whether it were I or they, so we preach, and so ye believed.*

This is the Gospel. This is what one must believe to be saved.

When the Philippian Jailer asks Paul and Silas, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" And they reply, "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved," this is what he had to believe. That Jesus is the Christ. That by His death, our sins are forgiven, in His blood, and in His resurrection, the promise of eternal life.

**Acts 8:26-3**9
*And the angel of the Lord spake unto Philip, saying, Arise, and go toward the south unto the way that goeth down from Jerusalem unto Gaza, which is desert. And he arose and went: and, behold, a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had come to Jerusalem for to worship, Was returning, and sitting in his chariot read Esaias the prophet.*

*Then the Spirit said unto Philip, Go near, and join thyself to this chariot. And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest? And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me? And he desired Philip that he would come up and sit with him. The place of the scripture which he read was this, He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; and like a lamb dumb before his shearer, so opened he not his mouth: In his humiliation his judgment was taken away: and who shall declare his generation? for his life is taken from the earth.*

*And the eunuch answered Philip, and said, I pray thee, of whom speaketh the prophet this? of himself, or of some other man? Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus.*

*And as they went on their way, they came unto a certain water: and the eunuch said, See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?* *And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.*

*And he commanded the chariot to stand still: and they went down both into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him. And when they were come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip, that the eunuch saw him no more: and he went on his way rejoicing.*

The Gospel that was preached to the Ethiopian Eunuch was of Jesus being the Christ as promised in scripture. Not his willingness to turn from sin. Not his making Jesus "boss" of his life. Nothing about himself. Nothing more than accepting the truth about Jesus Christ.

teachings.title: What one must understand to be saved
teachings.theme: The gospel that must be believed
teachings.summary: To be saved one must believe he is a sinner deserving hell, that salvation is a free gift, that Jesus died and rose, and call upon Him, trusting nothing of himself.
teachings.text:
This is what one must understand to repent towards God and salvation in Christ Jesus.

If you don't believe you are a sinner, or that as a sinner you deserve Hell and death, you won't accept the Gospel.

If you don't believe that salvation from the wages of your sin; Hell and death, is a free gift, given by God's grace and not of yourself, you cannot turn to believe the Gospel.

If you don't believe that Jesus is the Son of God, Who was made flesh, lived a sinless life, was crucified, buried and risen again, that we may have remission of sin and eternal life, you can't believe and be saved.

If you think that anything you do can justify you, or to lose that free gift, given by God by grace through faith in Christ, you aren't saved.

If you don't accept the gift from God in Jesus name, calling upon the name of the Lord to forgive you, a sinner, you cannot be saved.

teachings.title: Cornelius saved by believing before baptism
teachings.theme: The gospel that must be believed
teachings.summary: The thief on the cross and Cornelius were saved by believing on Christ, receiving the Holy Ghost before baptism and without turning from sin.
teachings.text:
Now let's look at more examples of those who were saved by faith in Christ, not of works, turning from sin, "avoiding sin," etc.

We have already shown from scripture that the Ethiopian eunuch and the Philipian jailer were saved by believing on Christ. There is the obligatory Thief on the Cross (**Luke 23:32-43**), who confessed Jesus was Christ coming into His Kingdom. His salvation is a definite example, but most caught up in damnable heresy will say he was a "special case."

**Acts 10:30-48** tells us of a Gentile, Cornelius, whom along with his house and friends, are won to Christ by Peter.

Through divine appointment, Peter begins preaching to them *The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ: (he is Lord of all:)*

(Note: Jesus Christ IS Lord of all. He doesn't need you to anoint Him. God the Father already has)

Peter continues with a recitation of facts surrounding Jesus;

*That word, I say, ye know, which was published throughout all Judaea, and began from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached; How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him. And we are witnesses of all things which he did both in the land of the Jews, and in Jerusalem; whom they slew and hanged on a tree: Him God raised up the third day, and shewed him openly; Not to all the people, but unto witnesses chosen before God, even to us, who did eat and drink with him after he rose from the dead. And he commanded us to preach unto the people, and to testify that it is he which was ordained of God to be the Judge of quick and dead. To him give all the prophets witness, that through his name whosoever believeth in him shall receive remission of sins.*

And, while still preaching Christ, they who heard believed and were not only saved, but bestowed gifts by the Holy Ghost.

*While Peter yet spake these words, the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word.*

*And they of the circumcision which believed were astonished, as many as came with Peter, because that on the Gentiles also was poured out the gift of the Holy Ghost. For they heard them speak with tongues, and magnify God. Then answered Peter, Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, which have received the Holy Ghost as well as we? And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord. Then prayed they him to tarry certain days.*

Also note that their salvation and gifts came before being baptized. Not after or a result of. They believed Peter's report and believed on Christ and are in Heaven today awaiting the day of redemption in the presence of the Lord.

teachings.title: Saved by confessing Jesus is the Christ
teachings.theme: The gospel that must be believed
teachings.summary: Paul, Peter, Andrew and Thomas were saved by believing Jesus is the Christ, while Judas, the one who repented himself of his sin, was lost.
teachings.text:
**Acts 9:20** shows Saul, who became Paul, healed of his blindness, filled with the Spirit; *And straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God.*

And in **John 16:16** Peter, when Jesus asks the disciples *But whom say ye that I am*? says; *Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God*.

Peter's brother, the Apostle Andrew in **John 1:41**; *We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ.*

Thomas, in **John 20:28**-**29**, when he doubted the other Apostles when they told him they had seen Jesus resurrected, upon seeing Christ for himself; *Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.* 

*Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.*

We have example after example of those saved by faith on the risen Christ, who believed and it was counted unto them for righteousness. Not of repenting from sin. Not because they tried to avoid sin. Not because of anything of themselves, but the declaration that Jesus is Christ.

There is one apostle who repented, however.

**Matthew 27:3-5**
*Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, Saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood. And they said, What is that to us? see thou to that. And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself.*

And we know how that turned out for that reprobate.

teachings.title: Faith Is Trusting God's Word
teachings.theme: The gospel that must be believed
teachings.summary: Faith is trusting God's promises because He cannot lie, beginning with salvation by grace through faith, and the just live by faith.
teachings.text:
*Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen....But without faith it is impossible to please him.*

*So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.*

Faith is trusting someone or something promised. Relying on the hope of an offer or covenant. Of belief in the unseen based on faithfulness of the one making the promise. The testimony given. Their word.

Faith in God relies on His word being true, His promises being kept. His end of the covenant being as a rock. God, who cannot lie tells us His word, and by hearing, we believe the report.

That is faith.

And the just live by faith.

It isn't a mystical force. It isn't will-to-power sorcery. If faith moves mountains, it is by the promise of God to move it, not our will but His.

The Hall of Faith saints written about here, the recitation of those people who the scriptures tell us believed God when He made promises to them, who were made righteous by their faith and did the will of God for a reward not seen. A promise to be kept. Blessings bestowed on future generations. But their faith held on His word allowed them the opportunity to do great things for the Lord. Because one of the many promises God makes unto us is that He is a rewarder of them that diligently seek Him. Beginning with salvation.

*For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.*

*That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.*

*For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.*

This is the first promise. Faith in this is the rock upon which Christ built His church. The Kingdom of promise that we trust in. The better country; *that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.*..*a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.*

We are dead in sin. But made righteous by faith, our spirit quickened. Given eternal life. For the just lives by faith. Literally.

But more, once justified, we live by faith diligently seeking Him in His word. Rightly dividing His promises, and being told His will. And by faith we are blessed and rewarded.

*Honour thy father and mother; (which is the first commandment with promise;) That it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth*.

These are some of the promises made by the word of God that we may know are true:

*Verily I say unto you, There is no man that hath left house, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my sake, and the gospel's, But he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time, houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions; and in the world to come eternal life.*

Or, *These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.*

Or, *He that overcometh shall inherit all things; and I will be his God, and he shall be my son.*

Just as Abraham was made a covenant, a son to Sarah delivered, and a blessing to Isaac promised. Just as Moses and David and the prophets were made promises they trusted, and were delivered by the Lord. Just as Jesus fufifiled so many of the promises made by God. So too, God has made promises to we who believe. Who please the Lord by our faith in His word.

*How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!*

teachings.title: None other name under heaven
teachings.theme: The gospel that must be believed
teachings.summary: Salvation is only in the name of Jesus Christ, so there is no ecumenical path, no saving by other faiths or works, and no Yeshua of the Hebrew roots movement.
teachings.text:
I overlooked this this morning, but it's an important doctrine taken from Acts 4 verse 12, where Peter tells the accusers in the temple asking him by whose name and authority did Peter and John heal the lame man, and Peter says under the Spirit, Jesus Christ of Nazareth whom they had crucified. Then he says:

*Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.*

This is very important. It is in Jesus Christ's name that we are saved, there is none who come to the Father except through the Son. There is no ecumenical path to heaven. There are none saved by other faiths, trusting in their works, praying in the name of another. Not the Hebrew roots nonsense about "Yeshua."

If you are looking for righteousness and truth, you cannot find it in anyone else or belief in any other power but that of the Son. The matchless name of Jesus Christ.

teachings.title: The Lord looketh on the heart
teachings.summary: Man looks on the outward appearance but God on the heart, which reconciles Romans 4 and James 2: we are justified before God by faith and before men by works.
teachings.text:
**1 Samuel 16** introduces us to David, son of Jesse and God's anointed.

Having taken His Spirit off of Saul, the Lord sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint His new king-elect. And there Samuel brings the heifer for a sacrifice, and invites Jesse and all his to the service. Samuel supposed Jesse's son, Eliab, who looked the part to the prophet. But the Lord says to him;

*Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart*.

This is an important doctrine, that reinforces the seeming dichotomy of **Romans 4** and **James 2** that so many struggle with. That we are justified before God by our faith and justified before men by our works. Our appearance. That men are respecters of persons.

**James 2:1-14**
*My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons. For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool: Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts? Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him? But ye have despised the poor. Do not rich men oppress you, and draw you before the judgment seats? Do not they blaspheme that worthy name by the which ye are called? If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well:*

*But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors. For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all. For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill. Now if thou commit no adultery, yet if thou kill, thou art become a transgressor of the law. So speak ye, and so do, as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty. For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.*

As Jesus teaches in **John 7:24**;

*Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.*

And so when David is fetched from the flocks he shepherded, Samuel anoints him. A man after God's own heart.

God knows our hearts and the spirit by which we do things. As we see Saul, who is discomforted and growing more and more bitter, no longer having the favor of God upon him, an evil spirit is taken him.

His servants decide he needs a harpist to soothe the king when his temper is raised, and knowing David is a skilled harpist, they send for him. Saul loves him as a son and makes the man of Judah his armourbearer. And David plays to calm the king down, the Spirit of the Lord upon the soon-to-be king.

teachings.title: Justified before God and before men
teachings.summary: Paul speaks of justification before God by faith and James of justification before men by works, so there is no contradiction and James 2 does not teach a works gospel.
teachings.text:
Abraham is the example Paul uses, given us in scripture as a lesson in justification by faith to God, by grace not of debt. That the glory in our salvation is God's alone.

But what about before other men?

A man may say that faith without works is dead, being alone. That, to men, justification isn't seen of faith but by a man's works.

**James 2:18-23**
*Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works. Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble. But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead? Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar? Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect? And the scripture was fulfilled which saith, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and he was called the Friend of God.*

*A man may say...* The overlooked predicate for the argument James makes in his epistle, written to brethren, the saved, to encourage them to good works. A man may say that Abraham's faith was shown in his works and thus he was justified to others.

But we know that scripture says it was faith that justified Abraham to God.

*For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God. For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.*

By comparing scripture with scripture we see that there is no contradiction, only context. That Paul is writing of justification before God in grace, while James is writing of justification before man, by doing good works in faith.

The rhetorical question asked by a rhetorical man, "Was not Abraham justified by works?" is answered by the holy Spirit in **Romans 4** and **Genesis 15**. Not before God, or he would have to glory. The boasting wouldn't be excluded. The law of grace would become one of debt.

The misuse of **James 2** to teach a false gospel of works is one of the great stumbling blocks to salvation and faith. But by comparison, context and understanding we see that there is no contradiction found, anywhere in the Bible.

teachings.title: Saved by faith, shown by works
teachings.summary: 2 Corinthians 5 is a longer form of James 2: we are saved by faith alone, but unbelievers who judge by appearance see our faith through our works, which wins them to Christ.
teachings.text:
And again, this is a much longer form of **James 2**'s "faith without works is dead, being alone."

Note that we have a tabernacle in Heaven for us by faith, but it is naked without works. To the unsaved who judge the world by appearances, respecters of persons, judging only the things they can see, being blind to the spiritual, are made to see by our works, which are reflection of the light, the mercy we've been shown.

We are saved by faith alone. We share that faith by how we live. And by being mindful of that, we get others saved, and also brought into that ministry of reconciliation with us so that then others can be.

Our letters of commendation.

teachings.title: James 2 is no snare for works salvation
teachings.summary: Read in context and compared with the rest of scripture, James 2 is written to the already saved and its rhetorical questions cannot overturn the clear doctrine that we are made righteous by faith alone.
teachings.text:
Now we come to the verses that are a snare to so many, where they justify works based righteousness, despite all of the mountain of scripture that assures us we are made righteous by faith alone, through grace alone, in the perfect work of Christ Jesus.

But, comparing scripture with scripture, and the verses in context, it's not difficult to understand, unless you're a natural man seeking to force the Bible to fit your preconceived notion, rather than letting it tell you God's.

First, what follows is a series of rhetorical questions and reasoning logic, designed to give example to what James has already preached. And again, it is written to the brethren, the author assumes it is to those already saved, to exhort and edify, not to get them to believe. Not to save them spiritually, but to those already saved, become more complete in their Christian life.

We do not receive doctrine from rhetorical questions or "a man may say..." reasoning, stripped of context. We get them from clear statements that do not contradict others.

For brevity sake I have already given argument above, with verses as to why this interpretation that we must do works to be able to go to heaven and have eternal life is damnable heresy. Scroll up. I may add to it as we study through this section, but if that's not sufficient for you, your argument is with God, the Gospel as given by Jesus and then shared by the Apostles, and clear, consistent verses, given again and again from Genesis to Revelation.

If you are trusting in your own works to get righteous or to maintain the righteousness given by God in Christ, you are damning yourself and being made debtor to the whole of the law which no one can keep perfectly. For there are none righteous no not one. Repent, and obey the Gospel.

teachings.title: Dead faith is faith that profits no one
teachings.summary: Dead faith in James is not absent faith but faith with no outward life to help the needy, since salvation is a free gift while rewards and deliverance from trials come from being doers of the word.
teachings.text:
What does it profit a man who says he has faith but doesn't do anything with it? Being a hearer of the word only, not a doer. James is continuing this theme, and as in the earlier verses, he is referring to being saved from the temptations and trials that arise from our lusts and sins. Remember, his goal is to educate believers into becoming more perfect, complete, Christians. Not to get people saved in the born again sense. Knowing the context answers the rhetorical question. Further, the example of this rhetorical question *says* he has faith. This is important. James is tying in the lesson that people generally are respecters of persons with the concept that we are to be doers of the word, as befits those who will be judged by the law of liberty. We aren't judged by our works and sin, as the debtors are. We are free in Christ. This is the context of the entire epistle. James has already told us that we earn crowns of life for our deeds. But salvation is a gift, unmerited. Grace-mixing isn't how any of it works.

The next hypothetical in James reasoning, if someone is needy and you basically just say "thoughts and prayers!" it doesn't profit them anything. It's useless. Dead. It doesn't do anyone any good.

Dead faith doesn't mean it doesn't exist, but that there's no life in it. Nothing to indicate it, outwardly. It's alone, profiting no one else. A dead body exists, but it just lays there. The same is the faith of a Christian who doesn't exercise it to help the fatherless and widows and the poor. See the theme? Understand the larger context?

teachings.title: Abraham justified by faith before God, by works before men
teachings.summary: Comparing James 2 with Romans 4, Abraham was justified before God by faith alone decades before Isaac's offering, which only showed his faith before men, so the man may say passage is a rhetorical device and not doctrine.
teachings.text:
Getting back to it; next we see James continue to use rhetorical hypotheticals to reason with the believer, in this case, "a man may say..."

*Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble. But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead?*

A man may say this. What kind of man? Saved? Unsaved? A respecter of persons? Someone who could reasonably or unfairly doubt your profession of faith by your lack of visible works? You see that this is a device by which to show what someone *could say*, in order to get at the larger point. It is not directly stated doctrine. A man may say all manner of things. For example, we know devil's are not capable of coming to saving belief in Christ. Yet here it says, in this hypothetical man's argument, that they believe and tremble!

It would take an extreme case of Nicodemus-level Asperger's to draw a doctrine that devils believe on God, as saved Christians do. And yet many draw doctrine from the very same verse! Amazing.

James continues the argument: *Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar?*

Was Abraham justified by his works before God when he was prepared to sacrifice Isaac? Well, no. In fact we know that's not the case. A fact James makes clear in the summation following;

*Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and he was called the Friend of God.*

James says, you see how Abraham's works shut up the hypothetical man, judging Abraham? That his faith was made complete by his works, in regards to being justified by men.

We know this is true, because again in Romans 4, Paul cites the same scripture James does:

*1 What shall we say then that Abraham our father, as pertaining to the flesh, hath found?*

*2 For if Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory; but not before God.*

*3 For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.*

*4 Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt.*

*5 But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.*

*6 Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works,*

*7 Saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered.*

*8 Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin.*

*9 Cometh this blessedness then upon the circumcision only, or upon the uncircumcision also? for we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness.*

*10 How was it then reckoned? when he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.*

*11 And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised: that he might be the father of all them that believe, though they be not circumcised; that righteousness might be imputed unto them also:*

Abraham was saved spiritually, justified before God, by his faith alone. Decades before his circumcision. Decades before bringing Issac to the altar on the same mountain in Jerusalem where Jesus would later be crucified.
